new_statements.quote: §120. Ebenso wie eine Reihe von Sudân- sowie westafrikanischen und Bantusprachen, wie das Hottentottische und Chinesische, hat auch das Nuba — ob ursprünglich oder aufgepfropft wollen wir hier noch nicht entscheiden — den musikalischen Silbenton. ‚Jede Silbe hat ihren eigenen Ton, resp. ihre eigenen Töne' (Westermann, Ewegramm., S. 37). [...] §123. Nach meinen Texten kann ich nur zwei Tonhöhen feststellen, deren Abstand (wie im Ewe) eine Quart beträgt, für Samuêls Stimme: [c] und [g], wobei c den Hoch-, g den Tiefton darstellt. Außerdem kommen zwei Schleifen vor, von denen die aus c zu g den Hochtiefton und aus g zu c den Tiefhochton bilden.
new_statements.translation: §120. Just like a number of Sudanic as well as West African and Bantu languages, like Hottentot and Chinese, Nuba too - whether originally or grafted on we will not yet decide here - has musical syllable tone. 'Every syllable has its own tone, or its own tones' (Westermann, Ewe grammar, p. 37). [...] §123. From my texts I can establish only two pitches, whose interval (as in Ewe) is a fourth, for Samuel's voice [c] and [g], c representing the high tone, g the low tone. In addition two glides occur, of which the one from c to g forms the high-low (falling) tone and the one from g to c the low-high (rising) tone.
new_statements.citation: Czermak, Wilhelm. 1919. Kordofannubische Studien. Sitzungsberichte der Kaiserlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften in Wien, philosophisch-historische Klasse, 177. Band, 1. Abhandlung. Wien: Alfred Hoelder.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The Kordofan Nubian of Gebel Dair (as spoken by Samuel Fadl al-Maula) is described as a tone language: every syllable bears its own tone, with two levels (H, L) plus falling and rising contours, tones notated musically throughout the texts. Dynamic stress ('Druck') is treated only as speech rhythm linked to the sonority-based 'Ausspracharten', and no source (Czermak 1919, Junker & Czermak 1913, Meinhof 1917/18) states a syllable position for word stress in Dair; Meinhof (1916: 77; ZfK 9: 49) adds for Nubian/Kordofan Nubian generally that the dynamic accent fluctuates freely ('schwebend', the same word heard with three different stressings).
new_statements.exceptions: Meinhof ZfK 8: 263 lists tonal minimal pairs (bŏl : bōl 'Hund', kọl : kōl, kūre : kūré, ti : ṭi) and notes that the interrogative form ends in low tone ('die fragende Form wie im Ewe den Tiefton am Schluss hat'); Czermak 1919: 77 says the tones are 'sehr schwach zu hoeren' in ordinary speech but a foreigner's wrong tones are noticed; Junker & Czermak 1913: 16 mark stressed vowels token by token with an acute but give no rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable-level lexical and grammatical tone established from dictated texts of a single speaker, checked by having him sing (cantando) and then speak each text with intervals verified on an instrument; 'absolute' citation-form pronunciations were elicited only for part of the vocabulary (Czermak 1919: 31). No phrase-vs-word stress distinction is drawn.
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary sources (Junker & Czermak 1913, Meinhof ZfK 8 1917/18, Czermak 1919) rest on ONE speaker, Samuel Fadl al-Maula, labelled 'Dialekt von Gebel Dair' and filed by Meinhof and Glottolog-era bibliographies under Dair. Czermak 1919 (Einleitung pp. III-IV) specifies that Samuel was born in Kurgul(-tetere), 'suedlich vom Gebel-ed-Dair', of a Kurgili mother and a father from Moridsoel, and calls his speech 'aus Kurgili und Murini gemischt'; the variety is therefore an Eastern Kordofan Nubian lect of the Jebel Dair area rather than verified Thaminyi of Jebel el-Dair proper, and no alternative glottocode can be assigned with confidence. Kauczor 1920 (read for context) is Dilling (dili1252). Kauczor & Drexel's 1930-31 'Daiersprache' may not be Dair Nubian at all (a 1994 Sudanic Africa snippet calls it non-Nubian).

new_statements.quote: p. 90: "Die von WAIBLINGER und von mir abgehörten Texte zeigen in ihrer Tonnotation auf den ersten Blick, daß wir es mit sinngebenden Tonhöhen zu tun haben. Die klanglich gleichen Wörter können sich eben nur durch die Tonhöhe unterscheiden, z. B. bol (fis) : bol (ais) usw. Diese Verhältnisse wurden schon von CZERMAK festgestellt, werden also hier nur noch einmal objektiv bestätigt." p. 91: "Außer der Tonhöhe könnte möglicherweise nur noch die Dynamik zur Unterscheidung dienen. [...] Da es sich um Einzelwörter handelt, so läßt sich inbezug auf Kontraste sowie rhythmische und metrische Verhältnisse nichts sagen."
new_statements.translation: p. 90: 'The texts listened to by Waiblinger and by me show in their pitch notation at first glance that we are dealing with meaning-bearing pitches. The segmentally identical words can be distinguished only by pitch, e.g. bol (f-sharp) : bol (a-sharp) etc. These facts were already established by Czermak and are here merely confirmed once more objectively.' p. 91: 'Apart from pitch, possibly only dynamics [loudness] could serve as a distinguishing cue. [...] Since these are single words, nothing can be said about contrasts or about rhythmic and metrical relations.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Instrumental (phonograph-cylinder) confirmation that pitch is lexically distinctive in 'Dair' (tonal minimal pairs bol/bol, kol/kol/kol); the summary (p. 11) says meaning-bearing pitch is certain for Dair. Dynamic accent (Starkton) is noted only phrase by phrase (e.g. the first notes of kol in phrases 3-4 accented, crescendo in e nele) and offered as a possible secondary cue; no rule for the position of word stress is given, and the author says the single-word material permits no statement on rhythm or metre (p. 91) and that the accent observations allow no generalisation (pp. 11, 103).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated (the general method, p. 18, marks only a dynamic Hauptakzent '>' and derives Nebenakzente from bar position; nothing language-specific for Dair)
new_statements.exceptions: none; p. 102-103 notes that in Walze 9 phrase 8 e nele the syllable ne, marked low by Meinhof, was heard as high and with an onset crescendo, i.e. a tone-vs-Starkton transcription disagreement, not a stress rule
new_statements.identity_note: Heinitz's 'Dair' material is a single cylinder (Walze 9, 13 phrases of isolated words, recorded with an Italian translation) spoken by 'Samuel' -- per p. 27 'Walze 9 wurde besprochen von einem anderen Manne gleichen Namens', i.e. not the Kenzi speaker Samuel of cylinders 1, 2, 5, 6, and per p. 90 n. 1 the tonal pairs were chosen 'mit vorbereitender Unterstuetzung des Herrn Dr. Czermak'. This is evidently Czermak's informant Samuel Fadl el-Maula of Kurgul, whose speech Glottolog files under Ghulfan (ghul1238), not Dair/Thaminyi (dair1239) -- the same identity caveat already recorded in this folder's for Czermak 1919, Junker & Czermak 1913 and Meinhof 1917/18. The label 'Dair' is the 1910s Hamburg/Vienna usage.

sources.note: Hauptstueck D 'Die Intonation' §§120-123 (pp. 76-78): the Nuba of Gebel Dair has 'den musikalischen Silbenton' -- every syllable carries its own tone; two pitch levels a fourth apart (high c, low g) plus falling and rising glides; tones marked with notes in the texts. Dynamic 'Druck' is mentioned only in fn. 1 p. 77 as speech rhythm / 'Schallfuelledruck' tied to the 'Ausspracharten' (Hauptstueck B); no rule for the position of a word stress is given anywhere.

Vgl. meine Studienfahrt p. 77'; musical tones present but shifting with sentence position (p. 50); Gulfan p. 57 'Ueber Starkton und musikalischen Ton gilt das bei anderen Dialekten Gesagte'. sources.note: p. 77, on Nubian (Nile and Kordofan) in general: 'der dynamische Akzent im Nubischen ausserordentlich schwankt. Man kann dasselbe Wort in dreifach verschiedener Betonung unmittelbar hinter einander hoeren' (fn.: Garko budule 'Hase' with three stressings); Klingenheben: 'Das Nubische hat den dynamischen Akzent, aber es ist gleichgueltig, auf welche Silbe man ihn legt' -- i.e. Starkton 'schwebend' as in French, not fixed; hints of musical tone. Not Dair-specific.

sources.note: 'Zur Lautlehre' pp. 259-263 discusses segments and then pitch: p. 262-263 'dass sich im Kordofan-Nubischen musikalische Toene finden'; Czermak found Tonhoehen in the Gebel Dair dialect; tonal minimal pairs (bol/bol 'dog', kol, kure, ti/ti); 'Es ist wichtig, dass die fragende Form wie im Ewe den Tiefton am Schluss hat.' sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Lautlehre pp. 7-18 covers consonants, assimilation, vowels only; p. 16 explains that acute marks 'betonte' vowels (a e i o u unbetont kurz, á é í ó ú betont kurz, etc.) so stress is marked per word in the data, but no statement on where the accent falls and no accent section (contents p. 7-18: Konsonanten, Assimilation, Vokale). Tone not yet recognised (Meinhof 1917/18:262 and Czermak 1919 say it was missed here).

sources.note: No phonology content. p. 542: only a word list could be collected, informants not able to give verbs or grammatical forms; pp. 550-551: dialect comparison with Russegger (Koldadji) and Rueppell (Kulfan), note that some Nuba pronounce f for k in numerals; no accent or tone marks in the list and no remark on accent for the Berg-Nuba. NB the sentence p. 552 'Ihre Sprache ist mild, vocalreich, accent- und kraftlos' refers to the Barabra (Nile Nubians), not to the Dair Nuba.
